mcqs.question: A `BinaryTree` exposes its raw `root` node so callers can walk `left`/`right` pointers themselves to get an in-order traversal. What breaks if the tree's internal structure later changes?
options: Every piece of client code that reimplemented traversal using left/right directly must also be updated
Nothing breaks — node field names never change once a class is written
The tree becomes impossible to traverse in any order ever again
Only code written in the same file as BinaryTree would be affected
mcqs.explanation: Exposing internal structure couples every caller's traversal code to that specific structure, so any structural change breaks all of them, regardless of which file they live in. Traversal itself doesn't become impossible; it's the coupling and duplication that's the real problem this pattern solves.

mcqs.question: You need to walk two lists in lockstep, comparing element `i` of list A to element `i` of list B, and break out early if a mismatch is found. Which style of iteration fits best?
options: Internal iteration using forEach on each list separately
Neither style supports comparing two collections at once
External iteration — hold an iterator for each list and advance them together in a loop you control
Internal iteration is always preferable regardless of the use case
mcqs.explanation: External iterators let the caller hold and advance multiple independent iterators in the same loop, and break out whenever needed — exactly what lockstep comparison with early exit requires. Internal iteration (forEach) ties each callback to one collection and typically can't cleanly interleave two collections or break early.

mcqs.question: While looping over an array with an index-based iterator, code removes the current element inside the loop body. What's the likely consequence?
options: The loop completes correctly and visits every remaining element exactly once
The array automatically resizes to prevent any indexing issues
This is always safe in every programming language with no special handling needed
Subsequent elements shift down into the removed slot, so the iterator silently skips the element that slid into that position
mcqs.explanation: Removing an element shifts everything after it down by one index, so an iterator that just advances its index next will skip over the element that moved into the now-current slot. This is a well-known hazard — some languages throw an error specifically to prevent silently wrong results rather than letting it happen quietly.
